I'm less certain here, but I thought publication lag would be incredibly important merely because of the utilitarian aspect of research. If we can't get published, we can't get jobs / tenure. Therefore it is smart to publish on something that you KNOW can probably get published, based on current trends. (I also don't believe the literature on diversity is anywhere near saturated, so in this causal model I don't take into account a backward slide because there are "too many" diversity pubs.) That said, I may be too bullish since the recent administration is negative on diversity; I'm influenced again here by local stories in my network, where researchers are pursuing diversity irrespective of the current administration's preferences.

I interacted it with black and female -- the personal characteristics I identified as main effects. I think just because people are publishing on diversity doesn't make just anyone start publishing on it -- it is a pretty personal topic, either to oneself or one's beliefs, so I think it would interact especially with one's own identity.

I also interacted the two time trends together. I don't think they are fully independent, but I believe that news would impact pubs and moderate (inflate) its effect.

I noted all of these as positive interactions. (Interestingly - I am meta-noticing right now that what came easiest to mind for me were positive main effects and positive interactions; I wonder if that is just the way minds work!)

The way I chose to think about it, social science and Black is a positive interaction because they feed into each other. A Black researcher brings a perspective shaped by lived experience. They have grown up with some understanding of what racial inequality actually feels like. But that alone does not guarantee they will write about it. It matters whether their field makes space for those questions. Social science does. There is a whole community there already talking about race, journals that publish it, conferences where it is taken seriously. So when you put those two things together, someone who has reason to care and a field that says this is valid work, it pushes things forward in a way that neither would alone.

Asian and White I chose as negative, but for a different reason. If you look at who is doing research, it is mostly Asian and White scholars. That is just the reality. So when you see a paper with those two groups, you are looking at the default. It is what most papers look like. And that default does not nudge a paper toward talking about racial inequality. If anything, papers that really dig into race tend to include authors from groups with a more direct historical connection to those questions in this country. So having only Asian and White authors signals that race probably is not the main event.

And natural science and Hispanic I also chose as negative. Natural science just is not set up for questions about racial inequality. That is not what the journals want, not what gets funded, not what counts as a discovery in those fields. So even if a Hispanic scholar cares deeply about these issues, maybe they came to science because they love it but they still carry all that with them, the field itself does not encourage them to go there. If anything, it pushes the other way. So that combination does not amplify anything. It mutes it.

records.theory_text:
For social science and female, I gave it a positive sign because those two things feed into each other. A woman has lived through gender dynamics her whole life. She does not need to read about it in a textbook to understand that inequality exists. But having that awareness does not automatically mean she writes about it. That depends on whether her field treats gender as a real research topic. Social science does. There are journals dedicated to it, conferences, whole subfields built around these questions. So when someone with lived experience lands in a space that says this work matters, it pushes things forward in a way that neither factor would alone.

For natural science and female, I went with a negative sign because the dynamic is different. The lived experience is still there. A woman in natural science still navigates a world where gender shapes how she is treated. But natural science is not set up to make that the subject of research. The questions that count are about something else, cells or particles or equations. So even if she cares deeply, even if she experiences inequality every day, the field does not give her permission to write about it. The personal impulse is still there, but the disciplinary norms push against it. They weaken what would otherwise be there.

For news mentions and paper mentions, I chose a positive sign because public conversation and academic conversation do not happen in isolation. When gender inequality is all over the news, whether it is the MeToo movement or stories about the pay gap, it makes the topic feel like something that matters right now. Researchers are paying attention to the same headlines everyone else is. That seeps into what they write. At the same time, when papers start talking about inequality more, it creates a kind of momentum. Scholars look at what is being published and where the field is heading. Those two forces feed each other. The topic stays alive in both places, and each one keeps the other going.

records.theory_text: I expect disciplinary context to condition the effects of both discourse-level trends and author composition, which is why all three top interactions involve social_science. First, the positive interaction between social_science and prior academic inequality trends reflects a field-amplification mechanism: when inequality becomes more prominent in academic discourse overall, social science disciplines—whose core theories and methods are designed to analyze stratification and injustice—are especially likely to incorporate and extend that trend. Thus, the positive time-trend effect should be stronger inside social sciences than in other fields. Second, the positive interaction between Black author share and social_science reflects a contextual activation assumption: standpoint-related motivations or sensitivities are more likely to translate into explicit racial inequality research when scholars are embedded in disciplines where race is already a legitimate and central analytic category. In technical or natural science fields, such motivations may have fewer institutional channels for expression. Third, the positive interaction between news inequality trends and social_science reflects agenda-setting dynamics: while public discourse may influence academia broadly, social sciences are particularly responsive to societal events, normative debates, and policy-relevant issues. In sum, I assume that social science disciplines function as an enabling environment that amplifies both temporal discourse shifts and author-based standpoint effects, leading to positively signed interactions.

records.theory_text: The three interactions I selected all reflect a common theoretical logic: that the predictors of racial inequality scholarship are not independent but are instead conditioned by one another through mechanisms of institutional context, identity salience, and agenda responsiveness. The most important interaction, black × social_science, rests on the assumption that positionality-driven research motivation requires institutional scaffolding to be converted into published academic output. A Black scholar's lived experience and personal motivation to study racial inequality is a necessary but not sufficient condition — it must be coupled with a disciplinary environment that provides the conceptual vocabulary, methodological toolkit, peer legitimacy, and receptive journal outlets to transform that motivation into keyword-containing publications. Social science provides precisely this scaffolding, while engineering or natural science largely does not, meaning the two variables amplify each other beyond their additive individual effects. The second interaction, news_inequality_mentions_3_years × social_science, reflects the assumption that academic disciplines vary substantially in their permeability to external social pressures. Social scientists operate with a professional norm of societal relevance and are embedded in institutional reward structures — grant agencies, journal editors, tenure committees — that are themselves responsive to public discourse. When media salience of racial inequality rises, these institutional transmission mechanisms selectively channel that pressure into social science research agendas far more than into natural science or engineering ones, producing a superadditive effect. The third interaction, black × news_inequality_mentions_3_years, captures a resonance mechanism rooted in identity-contingent agenda responsiveness: high-profile public events involving racial inequality — police violence, civil rights movements, legislative battles — are not equally salient to all scholars but are particularly motivating to those with direct personal and community stakes in the issue. Black scholars are more likely to experience such moments as urgent calls to produce relevant knowledge, amplifying their already-higher baseline propensity to study racial inequality during periods of heightened public attention.

These explanations invoke interactions involving intermediate mechanisms without ultimately grounding them in a curved response.

records.theory_text: The three interactions I selected for the gender inequality case reflect the same overarching theoretical logic as in the racial inequality case — that predictors of inequality scholarship are mutually conditioning rather than independent — but with important gender-specific nuances that arise from the distinct structural position of gender as a social category cutting across all disciplines. The most important interaction, female × social_science, rests on the same institutional scaffolding assumption as its racial analogue: positionality-driven research motivation is a necessary but not sufficient condition for producing keyword-containing academic output, and it is most powerfully activated when coupled with a disciplinary environment that provides feminist conceptual frameworks, methodological legitimacy, receptive publication outlets, and peer communities that normalize and reward gender inequality scholarship. Female scholars in engineering or natural science may be equally motivated by personal experience of gender inequality but lack the institutional infrastructure to channel that motivation into the specific critical vocabulary our labeling scheme detects. The second interaction, female × news_inequality_mentions_3_years, captures an identity-contingent agenda responsiveness mechanism: landmark public events in gender inequality discourse — #MeToo, the gender pay gap debate, reproductive rights controversies — carry differential salience for scholars who are personally embedded in the social relations these events illuminate. Female scholars are more likely to experience such moments as urgent professional calls to action, amplifying their already-higher baseline propensity to produce gender inequality research during periods of heightened public attention, in a way that male scholars — even those sympathetic to gender equality — are less likely to do with the same intensity. The third interaction, female × engineering_and_technology, introduces a suppression dynamic that has no direct parallel in the racial inequality predictions and reflects a gender-specific theoretical consideration: engineering disciplines impose particularly strong norms of technical neutrality and objectivity that function as discursive gatekeepers, actively discouraging critical social framing even among scholars who personally experience gender inequality. Female engineers may discuss gender in their work — addressing representation gaps, pipeline leakage, or workplace climate — but the disciplinary grammar of engineering steers this discussion away from the critical feminist vocabulary that triggers positive classification in our labeling scheme, substantially dampening the positive effect of female authorship that operates so powerfully in social science contexts.

Social science institutions strengthen the activation and expression of that motivation through feminist frameworks and supportive scholarly infrastructure. Public attention produces greater salience and professional urgency among female scholars, increasing their research responsiveness. Engineering norms suppress the translation of female scholars' experiences and motivation into critical feminist framing. These mechanisms locate the focal interactions in intermediate motivation, urgency, and vocabulary use; none is ultimately grounded in a specified nonlinear response.

The selection and ranking of second-order interactions for predicting mentions of racial inequality in academic papers are grounded in theories of social identity, disciplinary norms, and the broader socio-political context that shapes scholarly work. The social_science × black interaction is considered the most important because it combines two of the strongest individual drivers of research focus: the disciplinary emphasis on social issues and the lived experiences or academic priorities of Black authors. Social science fields, by their nature, are designed to interrogate power structures, inequality, and marginalization, making them fertile ground for discussions of racial inequality. When Black scholars—who may have personal or professional stakes in racial justice—are part of these disciplines, the likelihood of addressing racial inequality is further amplified. This interaction reflects the idea that identity and disciplinary culture are not additive but multiplicative; the presence of Black authors in social science contexts creates a synergistic effect, as their perspectives and priorities align with the field's focus on societal inequities.

The social_science × authors_race_diversity_score interaction is ranked second because it captures how diversity within a discipline already attuned to social issues can deepen and broaden the exploration of racial inequality. Diverse author teams bring varied experiences and viewpoints, which can enrich theoretical and empirical approaches to studying inequality. In social science disciplines, where methodological pluralism and critical perspectives are valued, diversity is not just a demographic feature but a catalyst for more nuanced and inclusive research agendas. This interaction assumes that diversity is most impactful when embedded within a disciplinary culture that actively encourages the study of inequality, thereby reinforcing the importance of both context and composition in shaping research outcomes.

Finally, the news_inequality_mentions_3_years × black interaction is ranked third, reflecting the dynamic relationship between public discourse and academic research. When racial inequality is prominently discussed in the media, it signals a heightened societal awareness and urgency, which can motivate scholars—particularly those from marginalized groups—to engage with these issues in their work. For Black authors, whose experiences and academic interests may already be attuned to racial justice, a surge in public attention to inequality can provide both validation and impetus to contribute to the conversation. This interaction underscores the idea that research is not conducted in a vacuum; it is responsive to the socio-political environment, and the alignment of author identity with public discourse can create a powerful impetus for scholarly engagement with racial inequality. Together, these interactions highlight how disciplinary norms, author identity, and external context intersect to shape the content and focus of academic research.

records.theory_text: My selection of these three interactions is governed by a hierarchical, structural-to-proximal logic, beginning with the foundational gatekeeping role of discipline and then moving to the more nuanced internal dynamics of author teams. The most important interaction, social_science × black, captures what I see as the essential synergy between motivational capacity and institutional opportunity. My core assumption is that a scholar's propensity to study racial inequality is not a simple function of identity or disciplinary context alone, but of their conjunction. A Black scholar carries, on average, a heightened personal stake in understanding racial subordination, but this motivation requires a disciplinary home that legitimizes such inquiry as rigorous scholarship to be fully realized in published output. Social science provides precisely this scaffolding-its journals, peer networks, and theoretical canons offer a receptive structure that amplifies the expression of standpoint-driven motivation. In a natural science or engineering field, an equally motivated Black scholar faces a disciplinary environment where the topic is defined as outside the scope of proper inquiry, thus dampening the effect. The positive sign therefore reflects a multiplicative amplification: the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. The second-most important interaction, social_science × natural_science, operates at an even more fundamental epistemological level. Its negative sign directly encodes the mutual exclusivity of these two broad domains of knowledge. This is not a trivial statistical artifact but a substantive embodiment of what sociologists of science call "boundary work": the categorical separation between disciplines that study social facts and those that study natural facts. A paper's location in one domain completely rules out the other, and since these domains have diametrically opposed relationships to the topic of racial inequality, their interaction provides a powerful structural constraint on prediction. Without this interaction term, the model would miss the stark, non-linear reality that moving from one disciplinary world to the other is not a matter of degree but of kind. The third interaction, black × authors_race_diversity_score, shifts the analytical lens from the macro-structure of disciplines to the micro-dynamics of collaboration. My reasoning here draws on theories of intergroup contact and collective knowledge production. Team racial diversity alone can be a superficial aggregation without genuine integration of perspectives; a high share of Black authors alone might indicate a team that is relatively homogeneous in its racialized experience. Their positive interaction, however, signals a distinct collaborative configuration: a truly multiracial team where Black scholars are a substantial, non-tokenized presence. I assume that this specific compositional form creates a generative tension within the collaborative process, where the lived reality of racial difference is enacted among co-authors, making the topic of racial inequality not merely an abstract research interest but a salient aspect of the working relationship itself. This reflexive environment, I theorize, is uniquely productive of explicit scholarship on racial inequality, yielding an effect that exceeds the additive contributions of its two constituent features.

records.theory_text: My selection of these three interactions is organized around a core theoretical principle: the expression of author positionality is always contingent on the disciplinary context in which scholarship is produced, and the most analytically powerful interactions are those that capture how institutional structures either amplify or suppress the scholarly potential of lived experience. The most important interaction, social_science × female, embodies what I theorize as the essential synergy between experiential motivation and disciplinary opportunity. My foundational assumption is that while women scholars, on average, possess a heightened personal stake in understanding and challenging gender inequality due to their direct encounters with sexism, patriarchal norms, and structural disadvantage, this motivation alone is insufficient to produce published research on the topic. It requires a disciplinary home that recognizes gender as a legitimate category of scholarly inquiry, provides theoretical frameworks such as feminist theory or gender studies, and offers professional rewards for such work through sympathetic reviewers, dedicated journals, and receptive collegial networks. Social science disciplines furnish precisely this scaffolding, creating what I call an "amplification zone" where personal motivation is institutionally channeled and legitimated. The positive sign of this interaction thus captures a multiplicative rather than merely additive effect: a woman in sociology does not simply carry two independent positive predictors but operates in a context where her standpoint-derived insights are actively cultivated. The second-most important interaction, social_science × natural_science, operates at a deeper structural level that I term the epistemological divide. Its negative sign encodes the hard boundary between two incommensurable modes of knowledge production. I assume that academic disciplines are not merely different in degree but fundamentally different in kind when it comes to their object of study-social sciences are organized around understanding socially constructed realities, while natural sciences focus on biophysical processes that exist independently of human meaning-making. A paper's location in one domain categorically precludes the other, and since these domains have antithetical relationships to gender as a topic of formal inquiry, the interaction provides a powerful structural constraint that a purely additive model would miss. This is not a statistical nuance but a substantive representation of what sociologists of science recognize as the foundational boundary work that constitutes modern disciplines. The third interaction, female × natural_science, shifts the analytical focus to what I theorize as a mechanism of structural suppression. My reasoning here draws on a rich body of research on the position of women in male-dominated STEM fields, which documents a paradoxical dynamic. Women in these disciplines disproportionately experience the very phenomena-bias, exclusion, chilly climate-that constitute gender inequality, yet they face strong countervailing pressures that inhibit them from making these experiences the object of their formal scholarly work. I assume that these pressures operate through multiple channels: professional socialization that defines gender-focused research as less rigorous or central, strategic career concerns that discourage being pigeonholed as "the woman who studies women," and the simple absence of mentors, reviewers, and departmental colleagues who would validate such inquiry. The negative sign of this interaction captures this dampening effect, where the motivation associated with female identity is actively suppressed rather than merely unrewarded, creating a silence that is especially pronounced given the heightened personal relevance of the topic. Together, these three interactions form a coherent theoretical architecture: the first identifies where standpoint-driven scholarship flourishes, the second demarcates the categorical boundary that constrains all social inquiry, and the third reveals where structural forces actively silence the very voices whose experience would otherwise propel attention to gender inequality.

records.theory_text: All three interactions share one underlying logic: disciplinary membership is the gatekeeping condition that allows other forces to express themselves as racial-inequality discourse. I treat `social_science` not merely as an additive booster but as a moderating context — an enabling ecology with the vocabulary, theoretical traditions, journals, reviewers, and reward structures that make naming racial inequality both legitimate and publishable. Outside that ecology (e.g., in engineering or the natural sciences), the same impulses have no sanctioned outlet, so their slopes flatten toward zero. This is why every interaction I selected is positive and why each pairs `social_science` with a force whose effect I believe is latent until a field activates it. For the first and most important interaction, `social_science × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` (+), my assumption is that the temporal "salience wave" of inequality attention does not lift all fields equally: when ambient scholarly attention to inequality rises (e.g., after 2013 and especially 2020), social scientists are positioned to ride that wave — reframing projects, launching new ones, and citing the moment — whereas a chemistry or mechanical-engineering paper is largely insulated from it, so the wave's predictive power is concentrated where the mandate exists. The third interaction, `social_science × news_inequality_mentions_3_years` (+), is the same mechanism operating one step upstream through the public sphere: media-driven salience translates into academic framing chiefly among scholars whose discipline treats public social problems as legitimate objects, so media climate matters far more for social-science output than for technical fields. The governing assumption across all three is multiplicative gating rather than simple addition: temporal climate, public attention, and authorial standpoint are best understood as potentials whose realization is conditional on a permissive disciplinary environment, which is why the interaction terms carry real, positive explanatory weight beyond the main effects.

records.theory_text: The selected second-order interactions highlight how disciplinary contexts and prior academic momentum synergize with author demographics to shape research on racial inequality. First, the positive interaction between `social_science` and the share of `black` authors is rooted in the assumption that while standpoint theory suggests Black scholars are intrinsically motivated to study racial disparities, the social sciences provide the necessary epistemological legitimacy, theoretical frameworks, and methodological tools to formally investigate these societal issues, thereby amplifying their impact compared to STEM fields where disciplinary norms may constrain such inquiries. Second, the positive interaction between `social_science` and `authors_race_diversity_score` reflects the assumption that while diverse teams generate a wider range of perspectives, social sciences are uniquely equipped to channel this cognitive and demographic diversity toward analyzing structural social problems like racial inequality, whereas diverse teams in other fields might direct their varied viewpoints toward technical or natural phenomena. Finally, the positive interaction between `paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` and `authors_race_diversity_score` is based on the premise of academic path dependence; a robust existing literature lowers the barrier to entry for researching inequality, and racially diverse teams, being highly attuned to these issues, are particularly well-positioned to recognize, engage with, and build upon this established scholarly infrastructure, creating a compounding effect where demographic diversity and academic momentum mutually reinforce the production of knowledge on racial inequality.

Social-science resources help translate Black scholars' motivation into formal inquiry; social-science orientation directs diverse teams' perspectives toward structural social problems; and diverse teams' attunement enhances their engagement with established inequality scholarship. These intermediate processes contain the proposed dependencies, but none is ultimately explained through curvature.

records.theory_text: The selected second-order interactions highlight how disciplinary contexts, team dynamics, and academic momentum synergize with author demographics to shape research on gender inequality. First, the positive interaction between `female` and `social_science` is rooted in standpoint theory and the sociology of science; while female scholars are intrinsically motivated to study gender disparities, social science disciplines provide the necessary epistemological legitimacy, established feminist frameworks, and peer-review acceptance to formally investigate these issues, thereby amplifying their impact compared to STEM fields where technical norms may constrain such inquiries. Second, the positive interaction between `female` and `num_authors` draws on critical mass theory, assuming that a higher proportion of female authors in larger research teams creates a critical mass that shifts group dynamics, reduces individual marginalization, and empowers the team to confidently tackle gender-related topics, whereas a lone female author in a small team may face greater pressure to conform to traditional, non-gendered research agendas. Finally, the positive interaction between `social_science` and `paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` is based on the premise of academic path dependence; a robust existing literature lowers the barrier to entry for researching inequality, and social science disciplines are uniquely positioned to absorb and build upon this scholarly infrastructure, creating a compounding effect where disciplinary focus and academic momentum mutually reinforce the production of knowledge on gender inequality.

records.theory_text: My selections for the most critical second-order interactions rest on the intersection of institutional structures, epistemological standpoints, and exogenous cultural shocks. I ranked the interaction between `social_science` and `female` as the most important with a positive sign because it represents the optimal alignment of venue and motivation; while the social sciences provide the necessary academic framework to study stratification, author teams with a high proportion of female researchers are theoretically more likely to possess the lived experience and epistemological drive to investigate gender dynamics. A surge in news coverage regarding societal inequality primarily reshapes the research agendas within the social sciences, acting as a catalyst for institutional funding and publications in those specific fields while leaving natural and engineering sciences largely unaffected. Finally, the positive interaction between `female` and `news_inequality_mentions_3_years` ranks third, reflecting demographic mobilization. When public awareness of inequality increases, author teams with higher shares of female scholars are historically the most active in translating that cultural momentum into formalized academic literature on gender disparities.

records.theory_text:
The three interactions I selected—`black × social_science`, `news_inequality_mentions_3_years × social_science`, and `black × news_inequality_mentions_3_years`—are united by a single theoretical conviction: racial inequality scholarship does not emerge from any single cause in isolation but from the *convergence* of identity, institutional context, and temporal-political opportunity, and it is precisely at the intersections of these forces that the probability of racial inequality discourse rises most sharply. I rank `black × social_science` first because I consider this interaction to be the most structurally fundamental. The underlying assumption is that the relationship between author racial identity and topic selection is not a simple additive main effect but is fundamentally *gated* by disciplinary context. A Black scholar possesses, through lived experience and community ties, what standpoint theorists (Collins, 2000; Harding, 1991) call "epistemic advantage" regarding racial inequality—an intimate familiarity with the phenomenon that generates both the motivation to study it and the interpretive frameworks to recognize it as a structural problem rather than an individual misfortune. However, this epistemic advantage can only be converted into published scholarship when the institutional environment provides the conceptual language (e.g., systemic racism, racial stratification), the methodological infrastructure (e.g., survey instruments for measuring discrimination, archival collections on racial violence), and the legitimating norms (e.g., peer reviewers who recognize racial inequality as a valid research question) necessary for such work. In social science departments, these conditions are met; in a biochemistry laboratory or an aerospace engineering program, they are almost entirely absent. I therefore expect a strong positive interaction: the marginal effect of `black` on racial inequality mention is substantially larger when `social_science = 1` than when it equals zero, and conversely, the marginal effect of `social_science` is amplified when the author team has higher Black representation. This is not merely a statistical convenience but reflects a genuine causal mechanism of *institutional enablement*: identity supplies the motivation, and discipline supplies the means.

I rank `news_inequality_mentions_3_years × social_science` second because it captures a different but equally important conditional mechanism: the *permeability* of academic disciplines to external societal shocks. My assumption here is that the transmission of public discourse into academic production is not uniform across the knowledge system but is heavily concentrated in disciplines whose epistemological mission is to understand and explain social phenomena. When a wave of media attention to racial inequality sweeps through public discourse—triggered, for example, by the police killings of Michael Brown, Eric Garner, or George Floyd—social scientists experience this as directly relevant to their research programs. Sociology journals issue special calls for papers on racial justice; political science departments organize panels on the politics of race; psychology labs accelerate ongoing projects on racial bias. In these fields, the boundary between "society" and "the academy" is intentionally porous. By contrast, a spike in news coverage of racial inequality has virtually no mechanism through which it would alter the research agenda of a condensed matter physicist or an organic chemist, whose work is governed by internal scientific questions largely decoupled from current events. The positive sign of this interaction reflects my belief that societal salience and disciplinary orientation are *complements*: news attention provides the stimulus, and social science provides the receptive apparatus. Neither alone is as powerful as their combination. I rank this second rather than first because, while the societal-to-academic transmission channel is important, I believe it is somewhat more episodic and event-driven than the structural identity-by-institution interaction, which operates continuously regardless of whether a particular crisis is in the news cycle.

I rank `black × news_inequality_mentions_3_years` third because it captures what I call a *resonance* or *mobilization* effect that operates at the intersection of personal identity and historical moment. My reasoning is that when racial inequality becomes salient in public discourse, this salience does not affect all scholars equally. Black scholars experience public episodes of racial injustice—police brutality, hate crimes, political backlash against racial equity policies—not as abstract news items but as events that implicate their own communities, families, and bodily safety. This personal stake generates a powerful motivational surge to contribute scholarly analysis, to document the phenomenon, and to intervene in public debate through academic channels. Simultaneously, institutional demand for Black scholarly voices rises during such periods: journal editors solicit commentary from Black experts, funding agencies create rapid-response grants on racial justice, and universities seek to demonstrate institutional responsiveness by amplifying the work of Black faculty. The positive sign reflects this dual mobilization—both internal (motivation) and external (demand)—that amplifies the effect of news salience specifically for author teams with higher Black representation. I rank this third because, while theoretically compelling, I believe its empirical magnitude may be somewhat smaller than the first two interactions. The identity-by-institution interaction (Rank 1) operates as a persistent structural condition affecting every paper a Black social scientist produces, whereas the identity-by-news interaction (Rank 3) operates primarily during periods of heightened public salience, which, while impactful, represent a subset of the total time window. Additionally, the news-by-institution interaction (Rank 2) affects the entire population of social scientists during salient periods, whereas the identity-by-news interaction affects only the subset of scholars with higher Black representation, implying a smaller aggregate effect.

A critical assumption underlying all three interactions is that the production of racial inequality scholarship is characterized by *multiplicative* rather than merely additive causation. That is, I do not believe that identity, institution, and context simply contribute independent increments of probability. Rather, I believe they function as *necessary complements*: identity without institutional support remains unrealized potential; institutional support without motivated actors produces generic scholarship that may not foreground race; and both identity and institution without temporal-political opportunity produce steady-state output rather than the surges that characterize moments of racial reckoning. The positive signs on all three interactions reflect this complementarity logic—each pair of features amplifies the other's effect on the outcome. I did not select any negatively signed interactions among my top three because I believe the most theoretically important conditional relationships in this domain are synergistic rather than suppressive. Negative interactions certainly exist—for example, `black × natural_science` would likely be negative, reflecting the suppression of identity-driven topic selection in disciplines inhospitable to racial inequality research—but I view these as the logical mirror image of the positive interactions I selected (i.e., `black × social_science` being positive implies that the effect of `black` is weaker outside social science, which includes natural science), and thus less theoretically distinctive to highlight separately.

The three interactions I selected—`female × social_science`, `news_inequality_mentions_3_years × social_science`, and `female × news_inequality_mentions_3_years`—are unified by a single theoretical conviction: gender inequality scholarship emerges not from any single cause in isolation but from the *convergence* of gendered identity, institutional context, and temporal-political opportunity, and it is precisely at the intersections of these forces that the probability of gender inequality discourse rises most sharply. I rank `female × social_science` first because I consider this interaction to be the most structurally fundamental and continuously operative. The underlying assumption is that the relationship between author gender and topic selection is not a simple additive main effect but is fundamentally *gated* by disciplinary context. Feminist standpoint theory (Harding, 1991; Hartsock, 1983; Smith, 1987) posits that women's lived experience under patriarchal social arrangements generates a distinctive epistemic position from which gender-based domination becomes visible as a structural problem requiring explanation. A woman scholar carries, through her own encounters with sexism, gender stereotypes, and institutional male dominance, what Dorothy Smith (1987) called a "bifurcated consciousness"—an awareness of the gap between the official, male-centered accounts of social life and the actual texture of women's experience. This awareness generates both the motivation to investigate gender inequality and the interpretive sensitivity to recognize it in empirical data. However, this epistemic advantage can only be converted into published scholarship when the institutional environment provides the conceptual language (patriarchy, gender performativity, the gender pay gap), the methodological infrastructure (validated scales for measuring sexism, qualitative protocols for capturing gendered experience), and the legitimating norms (peer reviewers who recognize gender inequality as a valid research question, tenure committees that value feminist scholarship) necessary for such work. In social science departments, these conditions are met and actively reinforced; in a biochemistry laboratory or an aerospace engineering program, they are almost entirely absent. I therefore expect a strong positive interaction: the marginal effect of `female` on gender inequality mention is substantially larger when `social_science = 1` than when it equals zero, and conversely, the marginal effect of `social_science` is amplified when the author team has higher female representation. This is not merely a statistical convenience but reflects a genuine causal mechanism of *institutional enablement*: gendered identity supplies the motivation, and social science discipline supplies the means. I rank this first rather than second or third because it operates as a persistent structural condition affecting every paper a woman social scientist produces across all time periods, regardless of whether a particular gender crisis dominates the news cycle.

I rank `news_inequality_mentions_3_years × social_science` second because it captures a different but equally important conditional mechanism: the *permeability* of academic disciplines to external societal shocks concerning gender. My assumption here is that the transmission of public discourse into academic production is not uniform across the knowledge system but is heavily concentrated in disciplines whose epistemological mission is to understand and explain social phenomena. When a wave of media attention to gender inequality sweeps through public discourse—triggered, for example, by the #MeToo movement (2017–2018), the revelation of widespread sexual harassment in academia and industry, political battles over reproductive rights, or sustained coverage of the gender wage gap—social scientists experience this as directly relevant to their research programs. Sociology journals issue special calls for papers on gender-based violence; psychology departments accelerate ongoing projects on the psychological effects of sexism; political science panels convene on the politics of gender equity. In these fields, the boundary between "society" and "the academy" is intentionally porous, and societal crises are treated as legitimate and urgent objects of scholarly inquiry. By contrast, a spike in #MeToo coverage has virtually no mechanism through which it would alter the research agenda of a condensed matter physicist or an organic chemist, whose work is governed by internal scientific questions largely decoupled from current events. The positive sign of this interaction reflects my belief that societal salience and disciplinary orientation are *complements*: news attention provides the stimulus, and social science provides the receptive apparatus. Neither alone is as powerful as their combination. I rank this second rather than first because, while the societal-to-academic transmission channel is powerful, it is more episodic and event-driven than the structural identity-by-institution interaction. The #MeToo movement created a dramatic but temporally bounded surge; the identity-by-institution interaction, by contrast, operates continuously across all years, producing a steady-state elevation in gender inequality scholarship among women social scientists regardless of the news cycle.

I rank `female × news_inequality_mentions_3_years` third because it captures what I call a *resonance* or *mobilization* effect that operates at the intersection of personal gender identity and historical moment. My reasoning is that when gender inequality becomes salient in public discourse, this salience does not affect all scholars equally. Women scholars experience public episodes of gender injustice—the viral spread of #MeToo testimonies, the confirmation hearings involving allegations of sexual misconduct, the publication of gender pay gap data, the rollback of reproductive rights—not as abstract news items but as events that implicate their own professional lives, bodily autonomy, and community well-being. This personal stake generates a powerful motivational surge to contribute scholarly analysis, to document the phenomenon empirically, and to intervene in public debate through academic channels. Simultaneously, institutional demand for women's scholarly voices rises during such periods: journal editors solicit commentary from women experts on gender, funding agencies create rapid-response grants on gender-based violence and workplace harassment, and universities seek to demonstrate institutional responsiveness by amplifying the work of women faculty. The result is that the effect of societal salience (`news_inequality_mentions_3_years`) on gender inequality scholarship is *amplified* for author teams with higher female representation. The positive sign reflects this dual mobilization—both internal (heightened personal motivation) and external (increased institutional demand)—that amplifies the effect of news salience specifically for author teams with higher female representation. I rank this third because, while theoretically compelling, I believe its empirical magnitude may be somewhat smaller than the first two interactions for two reasons. First, the identity-by-institution interaction (Rank 1) operates as a persistent structural condition affecting every paper a woman social scientist produces, whereas the identity-by-news interaction (Rank 3) operates primarily during periods of heightened public salience, which represent a subset of the total time window. Second, the news-by-institution interaction (Rank 2) affects the entire population of social scientists during salient periods, whereas the identity-by-news interaction affects only the subset of scholars with higher female representation, implying a narrower aggregate effect on the overall probability of gender inequality mention in the dataset.

A critical assumption underlying all three interactions is that the production of gender inequality scholarship is characterized by *multiplicative* rather than merely additive causation. That is, I do not believe that identity, institution, and context simply contribute independent increments of probability. Rather, I believe they function as *necessary complements*: gendered identity without institutional support remains unrealized potential—a woman scholar in a physics department may be deeply motivated to study gender inequality but lacks the disciplinary vocabulary, methodological tools, and peer community to do so; institutional support without motivated actors produces generic scholarship that may not foreground gender as a central analytic category; and both identity and institution without temporal-political opportunity produce steady-state output rather than the surges that characterize moments of gender reckoning such as #MeToo. The positive signs on all three interactions reflect this complementarity logic—each pair of features amplifies the other's effect on the outcome. I did not select any negatively signed interactions among my top three because I believe the most theoretically important conditional relationships in this domain are synergistic rather than suppressive. Negative interactions certainly exist—for example, `female × natural_science` would likely be negative, reflecting the suppression of gender-identity-driven topic selection in disciplines inhospitable to gender inequality research—but I view these as the logical mirror image of the positive interactions I selected (i.e., `female × social_science` being positive implies that the effect of `female` is weaker outside social science, which includes natural science), and thus less theoretically distinctive to highlight separately. The three positive interactions I selected collectively articulate a theory of *convergent enablement*: gender inequality scholarship is most likely when the right people (women scholars), in the right places (social science disciplines), at the right time (periods of public gender salience) come together, and it is the multiplicative interaction among these conditions—not their mere additive co-occurrence—that drives the highest probability of gender inequality discourse.
